items.description:
Craig Gauthier has worked in 33 countries, spent five years as a professor, walked out of a hospital job where everyone was counting down to a pension, and now advises companies on strategy and speaks on stages around the world. His #1 international bestseller Rules Optional came out this summer and it starts with one question: which rules are you following that no longer serve you? We get into why trust and attention are the two scarcest resources today, the fleas-in-a-jar conditioning that keeps people in a 9-to-5 nobody chose, and why he thinks plumbers will out-earn lawyers as AI eats knowledge work.

Then Craig runs his Break, Build, Become framework on me: getting laid off in 2014, refusing to go back to a salary, building and selling two accounting firms, and starting over with Taxifi. Along the way: why the online world is about to get commoditized while real-world experiences get stupid expensive, the three buckets of health, wealth and relationships, and why hunting for your one authentic self is a myth.

items.description:
Brian Claire got pushed into accounting by his mom, bounced through BlackBerry, the Ottawa Hospital and defence firms, then hung his shingle in 2018 and built Blueprint Accounting into a seven-person firm serving clients coast to coast. Along the way he kept running into the same problem: payroll tools built for one business at a time, not for an accounting firm running fifty of them.

So he summarized a Slack thread in Claude, pasted it into Cursor, and ten minutes later had a prototype. He showed it to accountant friends, surveyed 60 firms, found they were juggling five to six payroll platforms each, hired an agency to build it, launched to a room of 40 people with a live glitch, and signed his first paying client within six months. Then he merged with a developer who was building the same thing and rebranded to Nooma.

We get into why 300,000 accountants have left the industry, why the partnership model is dead, how a non-developer manages a dev agency, what to put in a shareholder agreement with co-founders, whether a payroll platform that replaces 80% of a person is still a $40-a-month product, and why Intuit might be coming for your clients.

He went on to study computer science and cybersecurity in Russia, then built his career on the other side: keeping businesses safe from the hackers he grew up watching. Today he runs a managed IT, AI and cybersecurity company serving 10-to-50-person businesses, the size he calls the "hacker sweet spot," and he wrote Hack Proof: A Guide to Cybersecurity for Your Business.

Three out of four cyberattacks are now AI-related, and most small business owners have no idea what tools their employees are pasting client data into. We get into his Simplify, Secure, Scale model, shadow AI, why your cyber insurance might not pay out, the $47 non-compliance fee that quietly voids your coverage, ransomware that locks your whole Outlook, the 200-day average before a breach is detected, and why "human in the loop" is the rule that keeps an AI agent from emptying your bank account.

items.title: What will we do differently next time?
After Action Review....Do it!
Why didn't things go as planned?
What was supposed to happen Vs What actually happened?
The 4-Question Meeting I Stole From the Military
items.description:
On September 30th my team at Taxifi ran our first After Action Review, a practice borrowed from the military where the team breaks down every deployment to improve the next one. I pulled out my notes from the meeting so you can take it back to your own business.

It's four questions: What was supposed to happen? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we do differently? One facilitator, no blame, everyone has a voice, and 40% of the meeting goes to that last question because that's where the action items come from. I walk through real examples from our review, including why we landed five clients instead of fifteen, and why a bookkeeper, an accountant and an AI developer in the same room will see the same month completely differently.

If you’re a founder, coach, or creator building something in the real world, this one will land.

items.title: Nobody Wants a Tax App: 5 Lessons From Building Taxifi in Public.
items.description:
This week’s Taxifi build update came with a few lessons I didn’t expect, and they’re changing how I think about the product.

Here are the 5 biggest takeaways so far:

1) Nobody wants a tax app. They want the problem gone.
2) Niche makes people lean in. The clearer the “who,” the stronger the pull.
3) Judgment free is a real feature. People don’t just need software, they need a safe place to start. (So many people apologize for being behind.)
4) Simple beats clever. The clearest promise wins:
“One-click, judgment-free tax filing so you never think about taxes again.”
5) Building in public changes how you ship. More feedback, more accountability, and faster decisions.

If you’re building a product, a brand, or anything customer-facing, this episode is a reminder that clarity, safety, and simplicity are the real differentiators.
